title: Nicholas Owen (22 March)
hook: a carpenter who built priest-holes in English houses and died under torture

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clement Hofbauer, the baker who waited years for his work to rise. Your line was the baker of vienna. What slow work did you leave alone? Day nine hundred seventy-six.

In some old English country houses, a guide will stop beside a fireplace, or a staircase, or a stretch of plain wall, and press something. A panel swings open. Behind it is a space barely big enough for a person to crouch in. Visitors call them priest-holes. They were built for Catholic priests to hide in when searchers came to the door, and some of them, tradition says, were built by one small man with a carpenter's tools. People called him Little John. His name was Nicholas Owen.
screen: `A PANEL SWINGS OPEN.` → `A SPACE TO CROUCH IN.` → `LITTLE JOHN, THE CARPENTER.`

segments.voice: In Nicholas Owen's England, it was a crime for a Catholic priest to say Mass, and a priest who was caught could be put to death for treason. Families who kept the old faith hid priests in their homes. Nicholas became a Jesuit brother, not a priest, and he used his trade. He worked, tradition says, mostly at night, alone, after receiving Communion, telling no one but the household. He built hiding places so well that searchers could tear a house apart for days and find nothing: false floors, hollow walls, spaces behind chimneys, sometimes one hiding place built to be found so the real one stayed hidden. Then he was caught. After days in hiding at a house called Hindlip, hungry and cramped, he came out, tradition says, partly to draw the searchers away from the priests still hidden. He was taken to the Tower of London and tortured, hung by the wrists, again and again, to make him name the houses and the priests. He never did. He died there. He was canonized with other martyrs of England and Wales. It was a cruel age on more than one side, and the Church remembers him not for hating anyone, but for keeping people safe. There's something fitting in his trade. In the Douay-Rheims, the people of his home town ask of Jesus: "Is not this the carpenter's son?" Nicholas Owen served God the way a carpenter can: with his hands, in silence, for other people's lives.
screen: `A CRIME TO SAY MASS.` · `A CARPENTER BUILDS AT NIGHT.` · `CAUGHT, TORTURED, SILENT.` · `HANDS IN THE SERVICE OF OTHERS.` · then, large: `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER'S SON?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use your hands for others. Settle, and breathe. Look at your hands. Turn them over. Think of what they can do that someone near you needs: fix a hinge, cook a meal, carry a bag, sew a button, write a card, hold a hand. Choose one thing, small and real, that you could do for someone this week, without telling anyone, the way Nicholas worked at night. If you pray, you can offer your hands to God for that work. If you don't, rest them open on your knees and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Nicholas Owen. A Jesuit brother and carpenter who built hiding places for priests in English houses, and died under torture rather than give anyone away.
Your line: the builder of hiding places. Today, do one useful thing with your hands for someone else, quietly, and don't mention it. Day nine hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Catholics in England and Wales remember Saint Nicholas Owen with the other martyrs of England and Wales, and the Jesuits keep his memory; visitors to some old English houses can still see hiding places attributed to him.

original.note: Greek: a builder or craftsman, the word for carpenter in Matthew 13:55.

trapdoor: what you thought: a priest-hole is a quaint feature of an old house.
what it means: it was a hiding place that could save a priest's life, built at night by men like Nicholas.
what a scholar hears: some hiding places in surviving English houses are attributed to Owen by their style, though that is hard to prove.

Confirm from John Gerard and Jesuit sources: 'Little John', working at night after Communion, decoy hiding places, capture at Hindlip Hall, coming out to draw searchers away, torture on the manacles in the Tower, death without betraying anyone.
Framing: 'a cruel age on more than one side' is meant to avoid casting Protestants as villains; Keeper and Anglican reader should check tone.
Trapdoor floor 3: confirm the attribution of surviving hides to Owen is largely by style.
